articles.title: People’s bodies are changing in the age of Ozempic. How are we meant to talk about it?
articles.summary: Discussing people’s bodies can be fraught. We asked eating disorder experts how to do so – or not – responsibly. In the age of Ozempic and people being open about plastic surgery, discussion about people’s bodies is rife.
body: It is a fraught topic. We asked eating disorder experts for guidelines to follow when talking about other people’s bodies, and how to do so without doing harm.

For experts in the field of eating disorders, the current ambivalence makes sense. “There’s a whiplash moment we’re stuck in,” says Dr Tom Hildebrandt, director of the Center for Eating and Weight Disorders at Mount Sinai hospital in New York.

The body positivity movement of the 2010s saw a mainstream push to “accept all body sizes, shapes and types”, says Hildebrandt. Then, with the explosion of GLP-1s, progress toward body acceptance “took a hard right turn”, he says – once again, “the media went through its idealization of weight loss”.
The vocabulary is different than it was before. Now, the focus is on “optimizing” one’s body and appearance, says Dr Ulrike Schmidt, professor of eating disorders at King’s College London.
points: In the age of Ozempic and people being open about plastic surgery, discussion about people’s bodies is rife.

articles.title: I’ve been told to apply to a civil and administrative tribunal over my faulty dishwasher. What does it involve?
articles.summary: Taking a consumer complaint to tribunal is likely to be onerous, writes policy professional Kat George, but the payoff may be worthwhile. A little over two years ago, I bought a new dishwasher. From the beginning, it did not function properly.
body: The retailer refused to accept a return for a refund or replacement, and because I bought it for my tenant, I had to replace it at my own cost. The whole process has been very frustrating, and I now have a useless dishwasher stored in my home, which remains under the manufacturer’s warranty.

I submitted a complaint to Fair Trading in a bid to force the retailer to engage with the issue, however the outcome was the same. Fair Trading says my next step is to apply to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT), if I am eligible. My question is: what would applying to NCAT involve? Could it lead to further costs for me?

Kat says: This is an extraordinarily frustrating situation. Under the Australian Consumer Law, however, you may have a strong argument that the dishwasher’s performance breaches the consumer guarantees.

body: The toymaker said its revenues had increased by 21% to 41.9bn Danish kroner (£4.8bn) in the first six months of 2026, driven by strong growth in the Americas, Europe and the Asia-Pacific regions, offsetting stalled sales in China.

Sales by its clients to consumers rose by 22% as it produced World Cup kits, including mini figures of players such as Harry Kane and even building kits of superstar players, including Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi which were retailing for up to £159.99.
Net profit increased 32% to 8.6bn Danish kroner (£1bn) as the group launched 330 new products including its hi-tech Smart Play kit, with bricks that emit sounds and light.

Niels B Christiansen, the chief executive of Lego Group, said: “We are very pleased with our strong start to 2026 and the excitement we see for the Lego brand. Our portfolio of products offers something for everyone, and culturally relevant brand experiences continue to drive demand across the globe. Our success in the market means we can maintain high investment levels in growth and sustainability for both the short and long term.”

articles.title: In ‘The Sun Never Sets,’ Dakota Fanning Goes Straight to the Heart
articles.summary: “I do find myself getting cynical about dating, but what I love most about Wendy and the film is that it isn’t cynical. It shows the reality of being a person trying to form relationships, and everyone’s doing their best.”
body: Dakota Fanning has spent much of her career being asked to prove that she has grown up. The premier child actor of the aughts has been burdened with the same narrow, repetitive narrative since 2000: How would she finally make the transition from a precocious young star to an adult actor?
“I think people get locked into a certain view of growing up as a child actor,” she says. “I hope that maybe I’ve expanded someone’s view of what it can look like.”

Fanning is calling from an apartment in New York, her whiteboard busy with a schedule of the scenes she’s due to film for a project she can’t talk about yet. She is as giggly and gracious as she seems on late-night talk shows, often addressing me by name—though that may have as much to do with her upbringing in Georgia as her many years of practice talking to the press.

Fanning’s younger sister, Elle, recognized her in the role immediately. “When she watched the movie, she was like, ‘People are going to think that they’ve never seen you in a role like this, and I think that’s true,’” Fanning recalls. “But she also said, ‘What they might not know is that it’s so you.’” Wendy, she adds, “is the person my family and friends know me as.”

articles.title: Have You Been Microcheating on Me?
articles.summary: Technology has made the parameters of cheating much harder to pin down. There’s physical cheating, obviously; then there’s emotional cheating, sexting, sliding into DMs, liking someone’s bikini photos, keeping an ex on standby—or what’s now known as “microcheating.”
body: I was on Instagram late one night, scrolling through the feeds of various models (I’m always looking for new and exciting ways to experience insomnia), when I noticed that my friend’s boyfriend was all over their comment sections, leaving hearts and emojis on a bunch of different girls’ photos.

Ew, I thought. Not because leaving a heart emoji is, in itself, some terrible offense, but because there’s something bleak about seeing a man you know in real life working his way through a stranger’s thirst traps while his girlfriend, presumably, has no idea.

According to basically every definition that comes up when I google it, microcheating covers a collection of small, subtle behaviors that violate the trust within a relationship without crossing the line into physical sex. They’re usually things you hide from your partner because somewhere, deep down, you know they’re wrong. That could mean texting someone and deleting the messages afterward. Flirting over DM. Going on dating apps “just to look.” Exchanging numbers with someone at a party. In other words, all the little things you’d probably be less inclined to do if your partner were standing next to you, watching.
points: Technology has made the parameters of cheating much harder to pin down.

articles.title: The Bride Wore a Dress Inspired by Degas’s Ballerinas for Her Upper East Side Wedding
articles.summary: Caroline Irvin and Samson Mesghena’s fall wedding was a love letter to New York City, with the bride wearing a One/Of dress to her Upper East Side ceremony and reception at the Rainbow Room.
body: Designer Caroline Irvin and investor Samson Mesghena first met when they kept crossing paths at the gym—the Equinox in New York’s Flatiron neighborhood, to be exact. She had been out of college for a few years; he had recently graduated from business school. After months of seeing each other in passing, Samson finally made his move in December of 2019, when he walked over and introduced himself. “I was immediately charmed by his ease, his humor, and kindness,” Caroline remembers. A few weeks later, he called and asked her to meet him for a drink. She didn’t need convincing.

After dating for nearly five years, they got engaged on a Saturday in November of 2024. Samson told Caroline that they were going to the Gagosian Gallery to see a Peter Doig show she’d been wanting to visit. “He told me to get dressed as we would be having brunch afterwards,” she remembers. “It sounded like a perfect Saturday!”
points: Caroline Irvin and Samson Mesghena’s fall wedding was a love letter to New York City, with the bride wearing a One/Of dress to her Upper East Side ceremony and reception at the Rainbow Room.

articles.title: A Brutally Honest Look at What Three Fashion People Bought—And Spent—In One Month
articles.summary: We asked three stylish people in or adjacent to the fashion industry to chronicle one month of their fashion consumption—and to note what was purchased at full price, discounted, and gifted.
body: Welcome to Show Us the Receipts, our recurring column on what fashion people really buy and spend.

Money remains taboo in almost every corner of life, but in fashion, dollars and cents can take on an especially complex dimension—from both inside and out. With a high buy-in to the luxury market and wages that don’t often allow professionals access to the goods offered by their own industry, we often find ourselves wondering how, exactly, our contemporaries afford their wardrobes. Do they come from generational wealth? Are they on every PR gifting list known to man? Are they savvy sale shoppers and bargain hunters? Or are they just really shrewd budgeters?

It was an average shopping month for the editor, who—save for the jeans and dress she was gifted—only made purchases via secondhand sites like Poshmark and The RealReal. And while she is happy with all of her purchases (even if she jokes, “I love heels I can’t walk in”), she does want to reprioritize her spending. “I want to spend less money on clothing, more on travel,” she admits.
